items.title: Origins of Bhakti & the Saguna–Nirguna Divide
items.body:
**In one line:** The Bhakti movement was a wave of devotional religion that put a personal love of God above caste and ritual, and it split into two streams — Saguna (God with form) and Nirguna (God without form).

**The story**

- **Bhakti** means loving **devotion** and a direct, personal bond with God, without priests or elaborate ritual in between.
- It first flowered in **South India (7th-12th centuries CE)** through the **Nayanars** (devotees of Shiva) and **Alvars** (devotees of Vishnu), as a **revival of theistic Hinduism** against Jainism and Buddhism, and later spread north.
- Why it grew: resentment of caste oppression under the varna system; the appeal to artisans and lower castes; the influence of **Islamic monotheism and Sufi liberalism**; and the fact that Shankara's abstract Advaita was too difficult for ordinary people.
- Over time it divided into two streams depending on how they imagined God — **Saguna** and **Nirguna**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The South-first origin, the Nayanar/Alvar pair, and the Saguna-vs-Nirguna saint lists are the most-asked framing questions on this topic.

**Picture it — the two streams**

| Aspect | Saguna Bhakti | Nirguna Bhakti |
|---|---|---|
| God | With form & attributes (Rama, Krishna) | Formless, attribute-less Brahman |
| Saints | Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Vallabhacharya | Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ravidas |
| Worship | Idol worship, festivals, bhajans/kirtans | Meditation, chanting (nam), rejects idolatry |

**Terms explained**

- **bhakti** = loving devotion to a personal God.
- **Saguna** = "with qualities" — God imagined with form and attributes (Rama, Krishna).
- **Nirguna** = "without qualities" — God as formless, attribute-less reality (Brahman).
- **Nayanars / Alvars** = the earliest South Indian Shaiva / Vaishnava devotee-poets.
- **Advaita** = Shankara's philosophy that the self and ultimate reality are one.

**Don't confuse:** **Saguna = God with a form** (so idol worship is fine); **Nirguna = God without form** (so idols are rejected). Both streams still stressed **equality, the vernacular, and a direct path to God**.

**Remember it:** Saguna = "Shape" (form); Nirguna = "No-guna" (no form).

**TL;DR**

- Bhakti stresses personal devotion and equality; first flourished in South India (7th-12th c.) via Nayanars and Alvars.
- It arose as a revival of Hinduism against Jainism/Buddhism and rigid caste ritual.
- Saguna = devotion to a God with form (Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Vallabhacharya).
- Nirguna = devotion to a formless God (Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ravidas); Sufi monotheism influenced its rise.
keyPoints: Bhakti stresses personal devotion and equality; first flourished in South India (7th–12th c.) via Nayanars and Alvars.
It arose as a revival of Hinduism resisting Jainism and Buddhism and rigid caste ritualism.
Saguna Bhakti = devotion to a God with form (Rama/Krishna) — Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Vallabhacharya.
Nirguna Bhakti = devotion to a formless God — Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ravidas.
Sufi monotheism and liberalism influenced the rise of the Bhakti movement.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Bhakti Movement in North & South India

items.title: South Indian Bhakti: Alvars, Nayanars & the Acharyas
items.body:
**In one line:** South India gave Bhakti its earliest poets (Alvars and Nayanars) and its great philosophers (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva), plus the radical Lingayat movement of Karnataka.

**The story**

- The **Alvars** (12 Vaishnava saints) and **Nayanars** (63 Shaiva saints) sang in **Tamil**, criticised the Brahmanical monopoly on ritual, and spread devotion through pilgrimage and sacred places. Alvar hymns became the base of **Srivaishnavism**.
- Three great philosopher-teachers (the **Acharyas**) then gave Bhakti its intellectual framework, differing on how closely the human soul relates to God.
- In 12th-century Karnataka, **Basavanna** founded the radical **Lingayat (Virashaiva)** movement, rejecting caste, temples and idols in favour of the personal **Ishtalinga**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The Alvar/Nayanar numbers and texts, the three Vedanta schools, and Basavanna/Lingayatism are high-frequency match and statement items.

**Picture it — Alvars vs Nayanars**

| | Nayanars | Alvars |
|---|---|---|
| Devotion | Shiva | Vishnu |
| Number | 63 saints | 12 saints (incl. Andal) |
| Hymns | **Tevaram** | **Nalayira Divya Prabandham** (4000 Tamil verses) |
| Woman saint | Karaikkal Ammaiyar | Andal |

**The three Acharyas (Vedanta schools)**

| Philosopher | School | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Adi Shankaracharya** (8th c.) | Advaita (Non-Dualism) | Soul = Brahman; the world is Maya. Founded 4 mathas — Badrinath (N), Puri (E), Dwarka (W), Sringeri (S) |
| **Ramanujacharya** (1017-1137) | Vishishtadvaita (Qualified Monism) | Souls distinct but connected to Brahman; founded the Srivaishnava sect |
| **Madhvacharya** (1238-1317) | Dvaita (Dualism) | Soul and Brahman eternally distinct; the world is real |

**Terms explained**

- **Acharya** = a founding teacher/philosopher of a school of thought.
- **Advaita / Vishishtadvaita / Dvaita** = non-dual / qualified-non-dual / dual views of the soul-God relationship.
- **matha** = a monastery/seat of learning (Shankara founded four): **Sringeri — Karnataka**, **Dwarka — Gujarat**, **Jagannath Puri — Odisha**, **Badrinath (Jyotirmath) — Uttarakhand**.
- **Ishtalinga** = the small personal linga a Lingayat wears and worships.
- **Vachana** = short free-verse Kannada poems of the Lingayat saints; debated at the **Anubhava Mantapa**.

**Don't confuse:** The Acharyas in order of "distance from oneness" — **Shankara (one) → Ramanuja (qualified) → Madhva (two/dual)**. **Alvars = Vishnu (12)**, **Nayanars = Shiva (63)**.

**Remember it:** Acharya order: Shankara (one) → Ramanuja (qualified) → Madhva (dual).

**TL;DR**

- Alvars = 12 Vaishnava saints (Nalayira Divya Prabandham, 4000 verses); Nayanars = 63 Shaiva saints (Tevaram).
- Andal (Alvar) and Karaikkal Ammaiyar (Nayanar) were prominent women saints.
- Shankara = Advaita, founded four mathas (Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, Sringeri); Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita; Madhva = Dvaita.
- Basavanna founded Lingayatism (Ishtalinga, Vachana poetry, Anubhava Mantapa) in 12th-century Karnataka.
keyPoints: Alvars = 12 Vaishnava saints (Nalayira Divya Prabandham, 4000 verses); Nayanars = 63 Shaiva saints (Tevaram).
Andal (Alvar) and Karaikkal Ammaiyar (Nayanar) were prominent women saints.
Shankaracharya = Advaita and founded four mathas: Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, Sringeri.
Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita (Srivaishnava); Madhva = Dvaita (soul & Brahman eternally distinct).
Basavanna founded Lingayatism (Ishtalinga worship, Vachana poetry, Anubhava Mantapa) in 12th-c. Karnataka.
items.mnemonic: Acharya order by 'distance from oneness': Shankara (one) → Ramanuja (qualified) → Madhva (two/dual).

items.title: Northern & Maharashtra Bhakti Saints
items.body:
**In one line:** Bhakti spread across North India through Ramananda's school (Kabir, Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira) and flowered in Maharashtra as the Varkari tradition devoted to Vithoba of Pandharpur.

**The story**

- **Ramananda** (c.14th–15th c.) carried Bhakti north, preaching Ram devotion in vernacular languages and taking disciples of **all castes** — the bridge from South to North Indian Bhakti.
- From this stream came **Kabir** (Nirguna, attacked idolatry and caste), **Tulsidas** (Saguna Ram devotion), **Surdas** (Krishna devotion), **Mirabai** (Krishna bhajans) and **Vallabhacharya** (founder of the Pushtimarga).
- In **Maharashtra**, the **Varkari** tradition (13th-17th c.) centred on **Vithoba (Vitthal) of Pandharpur** and composed **Abhangas** in simple Marathi — a chain of saints from **Dnyaneshwar** to **Tukaram**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The 'who wrote what' facts (Ramcharitmanas, Sursagar, Dnyaneshwari) and the Varkari saint-sequence are repeated exam points.

**Picture it — North Indian saints**

| Saint | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Ramananda** (c.14th–15th c.) | Ram Bhakti in vernacular; disciples of all castes (Kabir, Ravidas) |
| **Kabir** (15th c.) | Nirguna; attacked idolatry, caste, ritual; *Bijak*, *Kabir Granthavali*, verses in the *Adi Granth* |
| **Guru Nanak** (1469-1539) | Founder of Sikhism; Nirguna; denounced caste distinctions; began the **Langar** (community kitchen); three precepts **Nam Japna** (remember God), **Kirat Karna** (honest work), **Vand Chhakna** (share) |
| **Tulsidas** (1511-1623) | Saguna Ram Bhakti; *Ramcharitmanas* (Awadhi) |
| **Surdas** (1483-1563) | Krishna devotee; *Sursagar*; disciple of Vallabhacharya |
| **Mirabai** | Rajput princess; Krishna bhajans defying social norms |
| **Vallabhacharya** (1479-1531) | Founded *Pushtimarga* (Way of Grace); Shuddha-Dvaita |

**Maharashtra (Varkari) tradition — 13th-17th c.**

- **Dnyaneshwar (1275-1296):** *Dnyaneshwari* (Marathi commentary on the Gita).
- **Namdev:** hymns included in the **Guru Granth Sahib**.
- **Eknath:** *Eknathi Bhagavata*; tolerance.
- **Tukaram (17th c.):** reformist, humanist Abhangas to Vithoba.
- **Chokhamela** (Mahar caste) & **Soyarabai** protested untouchability; **Ramdas** (Dasbodh) guided Shivaji.

**Terms explained**

- **Abhanga** = a Marathi devotional verse-form of the Varkari saints.
- **Varkari** = the pilgrim-devotees of Vithoba at Pandharpur.
- **Pushtimarga** = Vallabhacharya's "path of grace" Krishna sect.
- **Adi Granth / Guru Granth Sahib** = the Sikh scripture, which includes verses of Kabir, Namdev and others.
- **Khalsa** = the Sikh brotherhood created by the tenth Guru, **Guru Gobind Singh (1699)** — not by Guru Nanak.

**Don't confuse:** **Tulsidas = Ram (Ramcharitmanas); Surdas = Krishna (Sursagar).** **Kabir is Nirguna**, while Tulsidas, Surdas and Mira are **Saguna**.

**Remember it:** Maharashtra Varkari "DNET": Dnyaneshwar → Namdev → Eknath → Tukaram.

**TL;DR**

- Ramananda carried Bhakti to North India and took disciples across castes, including Kabir and Ravidas.
- Kabir (Nirguna) criticised caste/ritual; works in Bijak, Kabir Granthavali and the Adi Granth.
- Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi); Surdas wrote Sursagar; Vallabhacharya founded the Pushtimarga.
- Maharashtra Varkari saints worship Vithoba at Pandharpur and compose Abhangas (Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram).
keyPoints: Ramananda carried Bhakti to North India and took disciples across castes, including Kabir and Ravidas.
Kabir (Nirguna) criticised caste/ritual; works in Bijak, Kabir Granthavali and the Adi Granth.
Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi); Surdas wrote Sursagar; Vallabhacharya founded the Pushtimarga sect.
Maharashtra Varkari saints worship Vithoba at Pandharpur and compose Abhangas.
Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari; Namdev's hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib; Tukaram composed reformist Abhangas.
Guru Nanak: Nirguna, against caste, introduced Langar; precepts Nam Japna, Kirat Karna, Vand Chhakna. The Khalsa was created by Guru Gobind Singh (1699).
items.mnemonic: Maharashtra Varkari 'DNET': Dnyaneshwar → Namdev → Eknath → Tukaram.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Bhakti in North India & Saints of Maharashtra

items.title: Sufism: Concepts, Silsilahs & Impact
items.body:
**In one line:** Sufism was the mystical, devotional side of Islam, organised into orders (silsilahs), that stressed love of God, service to the poor, and shared much of its spirit with Bhakti.

**The story**

- **Sufism** is **mystical Islam**: a spiritual journey, guided by a **pir/murshid** (master), to reach communion with God through love and purity of heart rather than law alone.
- The disciple (**murid**) advances through **maqamat** (stages). The **khanqah** (hospice) was the living centre — a place of prayer, learning and free food for the poor. After a saint died, his **dargah** (shrine) became a pilgrimage site, celebrated each year on the **urs**.
- By the 12th century Sufism organised into **silsilahs** (orders), which differed sharply on whether to accept state patronage and whether music (**sama**) was permitted.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The silsilah comparison (especially Chishti vs others on politics and sama) and the Sufi vocabulary are classic match and statement questions.

**Picture it — major silsilahs**

| Order | Founder in India | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Chishti** | Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, after 1192) | Love, tolerance, simplicity; **avoided politics**; embraced sama; Nizamuddin Auliya, Amir Khusrau |
| **Suhrawardi** | Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan) | **Close ties with the state**; accepted grants/posts; rejected sama |
| **Naqshbandi** | Bahauddin Naqshbandi | Strict Islamic law; opposed sama & shrine pilgrimage; **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** criticised Akbar |
| **Qadiri** | Sheikh Abdul Qadir | **Miyan Mir** enrolled Dara Shikoh & Jahanara |

**Terms explained**

- **pir/murshid** = the Sufi spiritual master; **murid** = the disciple.
- **khanqah** = a Sufi hospice/centre where Sufis lived and taught; **dargah** = a saint's tomb-shrine; **urs** = the saint's death-anniversary festival.
- **silsilah** = a spiritual order/lineage passed from master to disciple; **sama** = a musical gathering (qawwali) for devotion; **fanaa** = self-annihilation, merging with God.
- **Amir Khusrau** (Chishti, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya) pioneered a new poetic style, **sabaq-i-hindi** (the 'Indian style'), and used Persian metres in **Hindawi** (early Hindi) poetry.

**Shared social effects of Bhakti and Sufism**
- Growth of devotional literature in regional/vernacular languages.
- Softening of rigid caste barriers and stress on equality.
- Cultural interaction and syncretism between Hindu and Muslim traditions.
- They did **not** strengthen Vedic sacrificial ritualism — both movements moved away from elaborate ritual.
- **silsilah** = a Sufi order or chain of masters.
- **sama** = devotional music (accepted by Chishtis, rejected by Naqshbandis).
- **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** = Ibn-i-Arabi's doctrine of the "Unity of Being".

**Don't confuse:** **Chishtis avoided the state and embraced sama (music)**; **Suhrawardis kept state ties and rejected sama**; **Naqshbandis** were the most orthodox. A **khanqah** (a living centre) is not a **dargah** (a tomb-shrine).

**Remember it:** Silsilah stance on sama — Chishti YES, Suhrawardi/Naqshbandi NO.

**TL;DR**

- Sufism is mystical Islam: a murid seeks God under a pir/murshid, passing through maqamat (stages).
- Key terms: khanqah (hospice), silsilah (order), sama (music), dargah (shrine), urs (death anniversary).
- Chishti (Muinuddin Chishti, Ajmer) avoided politics and embraced sama; Nizamuddin Auliya and Amir Khusrau belonged to it.
- Suhrawardi kept state ties; Naqshbandi (Sirhindi) was orthodox and anti-sama; Qadiri's Miyan Mir taught Dara Shikoh. Sufis enriched vernaculars — Baba Farid (Punjabi), Amir Khusrau (qawwali, sabaq-i-hindi).
keyPoints: Sufism is mystical Islam: a murid seeks God under a pir/murshid, passing through maqamat (stages).
Key terms: khanqah (hospice), silsilah (order), sama (music), dargah (shrine), urs (death anniversary), fanaa (self-annihilation).
Chishti (Muinuddin Chishti, Ajmer) avoided politics and embraced sama; Nizamuddin Auliya and Amir Khusrau belonged to it.
Suhrawardi kept state ties; Naqshbandi (Sirhindi) was orthodox and anti-sama; Qadiri's Miyan Mir taught Dara Shikoh.
Sufis enriched vernacular literature — Baba Farid (Punjabi) and Amir Khusrau (Hindawi/qawwali, sabaq-i-hindi).
items.mnemonic: Silsilah stance on sama: Chishti YES, Suhrawardi/Naqshbandi NO.

items.title: Telugu Bhakti Poet-Saints (AP focus)
items.body:
**In one line:** The Telugu Bhakti poet-saints carried devotion into the Andhra country, founding Telugu devotional literature and Carnatic music — a core AP exam area.

**The story**

- The pan-Indian Bhakti wave reached the Telugu country through a line of poet-saints who sang in the mother tongue rather than Sanskrit.
- **Annamacharya** began it with temple **sankirtanas**; **Potana** turned the Bhagavata into Telugu; **Vemana** wrote sharp reformist verse; **Ramadasu** built the Bhadrachalam temple; and **Tyagaraja** carried the tradition into classical **Carnatic music**.
- Several of them link directly to AP's own history — Ramadasu served (and was jailed by) the **Golconda Qutb Shahis**, tying this topic to the Deccan sultanate story.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** These poets are heavily AP-examinable — their texts, temples and the Ramadasu-Golconda link appear repeatedly.

**Picture it — Telugu Bhakti saints**

| Poet-saint | Period | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Annamacharya (Annamayya)** | 1408-1503 | Earliest known composer of **Telugu sankirtanas** (~32,000) on **Lord Venkateswara of Tirumala-Tirupati**; *Pada Kavita Pitamaha*; works on copper plates |
| **Bammera Potana** | c.1450-1510 | Rendered the Bhagavata Purana into Telugu as **Andhra Mahabhagavatamu**; dedicated it to God, not a king |
| **Vemana (Yogi Vemana)** | 15th-17th c. | Aphoristic **Vemana Satakam** (ataveladi metre); attacked caste, ritual, hypocrisy; refrain *'Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema'* |
| **Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna)** | 17th c. | Rama **keertanas**; rebuilt the **Bhadrachalam temple**; jailed by the **Golconda Sultan Abul Hasan (Tanisha)** |
| **Tyagaraja** | 1767-1847 | One of the **Trinity of Carnatic music**; Telugu **kritis** to Rama (Pancharatna kritis) |

**Terms explained**

- **sankirtana / kriti / keertana** = Telugu devotional song-forms set to music.
- **Pada Kavita Pitamaha** = "grandfather of song-poetry", Annamacharya's title.
- **ataveladi** = the Telugu four-line metre Vemana used.
- **Carnatic Trinity** = Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri.

**Don't confuse:** **Annamacharya → Tirupati (Venkateswara)**; **Ramadasu → Bhadrachalam (Rama)**. **Vemana** wrote reformist aphorisms, not temple songs.

**Remember it:** Telugu Bhakti temples — Annamayya → Tirupati, Ramadasu → Bhadrachalam.

**TL;DR**

- Annamacharya (1408-1503): earliest Telugu sankirtana composer for Venkateswara (Tirupati), 'Pada Kavita Pitamaha'.
- Potana rendered the Bhagavata into Telugu as the Andhra Mahabhagavatamu.
- Vemana's aphoristic Satakam critiqued caste and ritual ('Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema').
- Bhadrachala Ramadasu built the Bhadrachalam temple and was jailed by Golconda's Tanisha; Tyagaraja (1767-1847) is one of the Carnatic Trinity.
keyPoints: Annamacharya (1408–1503): earliest Telugu sankirtana composer, devotee of Venkateswara (Tirupati), 'Pada Kavita Pitamaha'.
Bammera Potana rendered the Bhagavata into Telugu as the Andhra Mahabhagavatamu.
Vemana wrote the aphoristic Vemana Satakam critiquing caste and ritual (refrain 'Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema').
Bhadrachala Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna) built the Bhadrachalam temple and was jailed by the Golconda ruler Tanisha.
Tyagaraja (1767–1847) is one of the Carnatic Trinity; his Telugu kritis are largely devoted to Rama.
items.source: APPSC standard references — Telugu Bhakti poets (Annamacharya, Potana, Vemana, Ramadasu, Tyagaraja)

items.title: South Indian Bhakti in Detail — Hymn-makers, Acharyas' Seats and Works, Lingayats and Nathpanthis
items.body:
### South Indian Bhakti in Detail — Hymn-makers, Acharyas' Seats and Works, Lingayats and Nathpanthis

**In one line**
Exams test the poets inside the Nayanar and Alvar canons, where each Acharya was born or based, their key works, and the Lingayat and Nath figures.

**The story**
The **Tevaram** is the work of **Appar**, **Sambandar** and **Sundarar**; **Manikkavachakar** wrote the **Tiruvasagam**, and **Sekkilar**'s **Periya Puranam** told the 63 lives. **Nathamuni** compiled the Alvar canon; **Nammalvar** was the greatest Alvar; **Periyalvar** raised Andal, author of the **Tiruppavai**; the Alvar ideal was **prapatti**. **Shankara** was born at **Kaladi**; his mathas each keep a Veda (Sringeri the **Yajur Veda**, Badrinath the **Atharva Veda**). **Ramanuja** wrote the **Sri Bhashya** at **Srirangam**; **Madhva** founded the **Udupi** matha and taught a **fivefold** difference; **Nimbarka** taught **Dvaitadvaita**. **Basavanna** served **Bijjala**; with **Allama Prabhu** and **Akka Mahadevi** he forms the Lingayat trinity; **Madara Chennaiah** began the Vachana form; followers keep **Shatsthala** and **Panchacharas**. **Matsyendranath** and **Gorakhnath** led the Nathpanthis; the Siddhars gave **Siddha medicine**.

#### Tamil saints and the Acharyas

| Person / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar** | Nayanar trio whose hymns make up the Tevaram |
| **Manikkavachakar** | Shaiva poet of the **Tiruvasagam** |
| **Sekkilar** | **Periya Puranam** — lives of the 63 Nayanars (Chola court, 12th c.) |
| **Nathamuni** | Compiled the Nalayira Divya Prabandham (10th c.) |
| **Nammalvar** | Greatest Alvar — Tiruvaymoli |
| **Periyalvar & Andal** | Periyalvar = Andal's foster-father; Andal wrote the **Tiruppavai** |
| **Prapatti** | Total surrender to Vishnu (Alvar ideal) |
| **Shankara** | Born at **Kaladi** (Kerala), 8th c. |
| **Mathas and Vedas** | Sringeri — **Yajur Veda**; Puri — Rig; Dwarka — Sama; Badrinath — **Atharva Veda** |
| **Sri Bhashya** | Ramanuja's commentary on the Brahma Sutras; also Vedartha Sangraha |
| **Srirangam** | Seat of Ramanuja |
| **Udupi** | Madhva founded the Krishna matha (eight mathas) |
| **Panchabheda** | **Fivefold** difference — God/soul, God/matter, soul/matter, soul/soul, matter/matter |
| **Nimbarka** | **Dvaitadvaita**; Radha-Krishna worship |

#### Lingayats, Nathpanthis and Siddhars

| Person / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Basavanna** | Minister of the Kalachuri king **Bijjala** (Kalyana, 12th c.) |
| **Allama Prabhu** | Vachana mystic; presided over the Anubhava Mantapa |
| **Akka Mahadevi** | Woman Vachana poet, devotee of Chennamallikarjuna |
| **Madara Chennaiah** | Father of Vachana poetry (a cobbler) |
| **Shatsthala / Panchacharas** | Six stages of realisation / five codes of conduct |
| **Nathpanthis** | Founded by **Matsyendranath**, developed by **Gorakhnath** (hatha yoga) |
| **Siddhars** | Eighteen Siddhars — **Siddha medicine** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Tevaram** (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar) ≠ **Tiruvasagam** (Manikkavachakar) ≠ **Periya Puranam** (Sekkilar).
- **Nimbarka** = Dvaitadvaita; **Vallabha** = Shuddhadvaita; **Madhva** = Dvaita.
- Shankara was born at **Kaladi** (Kerala); Madhva's seat is **Udupi** (Karnataka).

**TL;DR**
- Tevaram — Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar; Tiruvasagam — Manikkavachakar; Periya Puranam — Sekkilar.
- Nathamuni compiled the Divya Prabandham; Nammalvar greatest Alvar; Andal — Tiruppavai.
- Shankara — Kaladi; Ramanuja — Sri Bhashya, Srirangam; Madhva — Udupi, panchabheda; Nimbarka — Dvaitadvaita.
- Basavanna (minister of Bijjala), Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi; Madara Chennaiah; Nathpanthis — Matsyendranath, Gorakhnath.
keyPoints: Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar composed the Tevaram; Sekkilar wrote the Periya Puranam.
Andal, foster-daughter of Periyalvar, wrote the Tiruppavai; Nathamuni compiled the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
Shankara was born at Kaladi (Kerala); Ramanuja wrote the Sri Bhashya; Madhva founded the Udupi matha; Nimbarka taught Dvaitadvaita.
Basavanna was a minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala; Akka Mahadevi was the woman Vachana poet.
The Nathpanthis were founded by Matsyendranath and developed by Gorakhnath.

items.title: Saints of Maharashtra in Detail — Works, Families and Crafts
items.body:
### Saints of Maharashtra in Detail — Works, Families and Crafts

**In one line**
Beyond the big four, exams ask which saint was a Mahar, a potter or a goldsmith, who wrote the Dasbodh, and what Dnyaneshwar and Eknath wrote besides their famous works.

**The story**
**Dnyaneshwar** wrote the **Amrutanubhav** besides the Dnyaneshwari, guided by his brother **Nivruttinath**. **Eknath**, pupil of **Janardan Swami**, wrote the **Bhavarth Ramayana**. **Tukaram** lived at **Dehu**. **Chokhamela**, a **Mahar**, and his wife **Soyarabai** sang against untouchability; **Bahina Bai** followed Tukaram; **Gora Kumbhar** was a potter, **Narhari Sonar** a goldsmith and **Kanhopatra** a courtesan's daughter; **Bhanudas** revived the Pandharpur temple. **Samarth Ramdas** founded the **Samarth Sampradaya** and wrote the **Dasbodh**.

#### Maharashtra saints

| Saint | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Dnyaneshwar** | 1275–1296 | **Amrutanubhav**; Nath tradition; Dnyaneshwari |
| **Nivruttinath** | — | Dnyaneshwar's elder brother and guru |
| **Eknath** | 1533–1599 | **Bhavarth Ramayana**, Rukmini Swayamwar; guru **Janardan Swami** |
| **Tukaram** | 17th c. | Lived at **Dehu**; Abhangas; rejected monastic life |
| **Chokhamela** | 14th c. | **Mahar**-caste saint; Abhangas against untouchability |
| **Soyarabai** | 14th c. | Chokhamela's wife; 'Chokha's Mahari'; Nirmala was his sister |
| **Bahina Bai** | 1628–1700 | Woman Varkari poet, devotee of Tukaram |
| **Gora Kumbhar** | — | Potter-saint of Ter |
| **Narhari Sonar** | — | Goldsmith-saint of Pandharpur |
| **Kanhopatra** | — | Courtesan's daughter who became a Varkari saint |
| **Bhanudas** | 1448–1513 | Revived the Pandharpur Vithoba temple |
| **Samarth Ramdas** | 1608–1681 | **Samarth Sampradaya**; **Dasbodh**, Manache Shlok; guide of Shivaji |

**Don't confuse**
- **Dasbodh** = Samarth Ramdas; **Dnyaneshwari** = Dnyaneshwar; **Bhavarth Ramayana** = Eknath.
- **Chokhamela** (Mahar), **Gora Kumbhar** (potter), **Narhari Sonar** (goldsmith) — saints from working communities.

**TL;DR**
- Dnyaneshwar — Amrutanubhav (guru Nivruttinath); Eknath — Bhavarth Ramayana (guru Janardan Swami); Tukaram — Dehu.
- Chokhamela (Mahar), Soyarabai, Bahina Bai, Gora Kumbhar, Narhari Sonar, Kanhopatra, Bhanudas.
- Samarth Ramdas — Dasbodh, Samarth Sampradaya.
keyPoints: Dnyaneshwar also wrote the Amrutanubhav; Eknath wrote the Bhavarth Ramayana, guided by Janardan Swami.
Chokhamela, a Mahar-caste saint, and his wife Soyarabai protested untouchability.
Gora Kumbhar was a potter-saint and Narhari Sonar a goldsmith-saint.
Samarth Ramdas founded the Samarth Sampradaya and wrote the Dasbodh.

items.title: North and East Indian Saints, the Chishti Lineage and Sufi Vocabulary in Detail
items.body:
### North and East Indian Saints, the Chishti Lineage and Sufi Vocabulary in Detail

**In one line**
More saints (Ravidas, Sankardev, Chaitanya, Dadu), the chain of Chishti masters after Muinuddin, the smaller orders, and the full list of Sufi terms exams pick from.

**The story**
**Kabir** was raised by **Neema**, a **weaver**'s wife, and spoke in **ulatbansi**. **Ravidas** was a **leather**-worker; tradition calls him the **guru of Mirabai**. Tulsidas started the **Ramleela** and the **Sankatmochan** temple; **Vallabha** taught **Shuddhadvaita**. In Assam **Sankardev** founded **Ekasarana** Dharma with **namghar**s and **Borgeet**; in Bengal **Chaitanya** spread **Gaudiya** Vaishnavism; in Rajasthan **Dadu** founded his panth. **Ramananda** is placed in the **14th**–15th century. After Muinuddin came **Bakhtiyar Kaki** at Delhi, **Baba Farid** (**Punjabi**), **Nizamuddin Auliya** (who saw **seven** sultans), **Chiragh-i-Delhi**, **Hamiduddin** and **Salim Chishti**. **Shihabuddin Suhrawardi** founded the Suhrawardis; the **Firdausi** (**Maneri**) and **Rishi** (**Nuruddin**) orders grew in Bihar and Kashmir. **Ibn-i-Arabi** gave Wahdat-ul-Wujud; Sirhindi replied with **Wahdat-ul-Shuhud**; the **Amrita Kunda** was translated. Terms: **Zikr**, **Tauba**, **Khalifa**, **Ziyarat**, **Hal**, **Biddat**.

#### North and East Indian saints

| Saint | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Kabir** | 15th c. | Raised by **Neema** and Niru, a Muslim **weaver** family of Varanasi |
| **Ulatbansi** | — | Kabir's cryptic 'upside-down' sayings |
| **Ravidas** | 15th–16th c. | **Leather**-worker (cobbler) saint; verses in the Guru Granth Sahib |
| **Mirabai** | 16th c. | Rajput princess of Mewar; tradition calls Ravidas the **guru of Mirabai** |
| **Tulsidas** | 16th c. | **Sankatmochan** temple (Varanasi); **Ramleela** tradition |
| **Vallabhacharya** | 1479–1531 | **Shuddhadvaita**; Pushtimarga (the PDF glosses it as "pure dualism") |
| **Sankardev** | 1449–1568 | **Ekasarana** Dharma (neo-Vaishnavism), Assam |
| **Namghar / sattra / Borgeet** | — | **Namghar**s (prayer halls), sattras (monasteries), **Borgeet** songs, Ankiya Naat plays |
| **Chaitanya** | 1486–1534 | **Gaudiya** Vaishnavism; sankirtan; later life at Puri |
| **Dadu Dayal** | 1544–1603 | Nirguna saint; **Dadu** Panth (Rajasthan) |
| **Ramananda** | 14th–15th c. | Standard dating (the PDF gives 1486–1533, which would post-date his pupil Kabir) |

#### Sufi saints, orders and terms

| Saint / term | Order | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** | Chishti | Muinuddin's successor at Delhi (Mehrauli) |
| **Baba Farid** | Chishti | Ganj-i-Shakar of Pakpattan; **Punjabi** verses in the Adi Granth |
| **Nizamuddin Auliya** | Chishti | Delhi; lived under **seven** sultans; fed the poor |
| **Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Delhi** | Chishti | 'Lamp of Delhi'; successor of Nizamuddin |
| **Hamiduddin Nagauri** | Chishti | Persian mystic poetry into Hindawi |
| **Salim Chishti** | Chishti | Sikri; Akbar's son Salim named after him |
| **Suhrawardi** | — | Founder **Shihabuddin Suhrawardi**; in India Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan) |
| **Firdausi** | Bihar | Suhrawardi branch; Sharfuddin Yahya **Maneri** |
| **Rishi order** | Kashmir | Shaikh **Nuruddin** Wali (Nund Rishi); Shaiva influence |
| **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** | — | 'Unity of being' — **Ibn-i-Arabi** |
| **Wahdat-ul-Shuhud** | — | 'Unity of appearance' — Sirhindi (Naqshbandi), 'Mujaddid' |
| **Amrita Kunda** | — | Yogic text translated into Arabic and Persian |
| **Zikr** | Term | Recitation of God's name |
| **Tauba** | Term | Repentance |
| **Khalifa** | Term | Disciple chosen as deputy/successor of the pir |
| **Ziyarat** | Term | Pilgrimage to a saint's tomb |
| **Hal** | Term | Mystical state (ecstasy) |
| **Biddat** | Term | Innovation against orthodoxy |

**Don't confuse**
- **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** (Ibn-i-Arabi, unity of being) ≠ **Wahdat-ul-Shuhud** (Sirhindi, unity of appearance).
- **Bakhtiyar Kaki** (Delhi) → **Baba Farid** (Pakpattan) → **Nizamuddin** (Delhi) → **Chiragh-i-Delhi** — the Chishti chain.
- **Sankardev** (Assam) ≠ **Shankaracharya** (Kerala, Advaita).

**TL;DR**
- Kabir (Neema, weaver; ulatbansi); Ravidas (leather-worker); Tulsidas (Ramleela, Sankatmochan); Vallabha (Shuddhadvaita).
- Sankardev — Ekasarana, namghar, Borgeet; Chaitanya — Gaudiya; Dadu Panth.
- Chishti chain: Muinuddin → Bakhtiyar Kaki → Baba Farid → Nizamuddin Auliya → Chiragh-i-Delhi; Salim Chishti.
- Firdausi (Maneri, Bihar); Rishi (Nuruddin, Kashmir); Ibn-i-Arabi vs Sirhindi.
- Terms: zikr, tauba, khalifa, ziyarat, hal, biddat.
keyPoints: Kabir was raised by a Muslim weaver couple; Ravidas was a leather-worker saint.
Sankardev founded Ekasarana Dharma in Assam with namghars; Chaitanya spread Gaudiya Vaishnavism; Vallabhacharya taught Shuddhadvaita.
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid, Nizamuddin Auliya and Chiragh-i-Delhi are the Chishti chain after Muinuddin.
The Rishi order of Kashmir was founded by Nuruddin Wali; the Firdausi order in Bihar by the circle of Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri.
Ibn-i-Arabi developed Wahdat-ul-Wujud; Sirhindi preached Wahdat-ul-Shuhud; zikr is the recitation of God's name.

items.title: The Ten Sikh Gurus and More Telugu Bhakti Poets
items.body:
### The Ten Sikh Gurus and More Telugu Bhakti Poets

**In one line**
Each Sikh Guru carries one exam fact (script, manjis, Amritsar, Adi Granth, Akal Takht, Khalsa), and the Telugu Bhakti list goes beyond Annamacharya to Kshetrayya, Vengamamba and Siddhendra Yogi.

**The story**
**Guru Nanak** was born at **Talwandi** and enlightened at **Sultanpur**. **Angad** standardised **Gurmukhi**; **Amardas** made **22 manjis**; **Ramdas** founded Amritsar and the **Anand Karaj**; **Arjan** compiled the **Adi Granth** (**1604**); **Hargobind** gave **Miri-Piri** and the **Akal Takht**; **Har Rai** sheltered Dara; Har Krishan is honoured at **Bangla Sahib**; Tegh Bahadur at **Sis Ganj**; **Gobind Singh** created the **Khalsa** (**1699**) with the five Ks (**kesh** to **kirpan**), finished the Granth at **Damdama** and died at **Nanded**. In Andhra, **Annamacharya** of **Tallapaka** sang **adhyatma** and **sringara** songs; **Kshetrayya** of **Movva** wrote padams; **Vengamamba** sang at Tirumala; **Narayana Tirtha** wrote the **Krishna Leela Tarangini**; **Siddhendra** Yogi wrote **Bhama Kalapam**; **Tyagaraja** lived at **Tiruvaiyaru**; Vemana's refrain is **Viswadabhirama**.

#### The Sikh Gurus

| Guru / place | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Guru Nanak** | 1469–1539 | Born **Talwandi** (Nankana Sahib); enlightenment at **Sultanpur** (1496); settled at Kartarpur |
| **2. Guru Angad** | 1539–1552 | Bhai Lehna; standardised **Gurmukhi**; Mall Akhara |
| **3. Guru Amardas** | 1552–1574 | **22 manjis**; against sati and purdah; persuaded Akbar to drop the pilgrim tax |
| **4. Guru Ramdas** | 1574–1581 | Founded Ramdaspur (Amritsar); **Anand Karaj** (Lavan) |
| **5. Guru Arjan Dev** | 1581–1606 | Compiled the **Adi Granth** (**1604**); Harmandir Sahib; first martyr (1606) |
| **6. Guru Hargobind** | 1606–1644 | **Miri-Piri** (two swords); **Akal Takht**; martial turn |
| **7. Guru Har Rai** | 1644–1661 | Sheltered Dara Shikoh |
| **8. Guru Har Krishan** | 1661–1664 | Child Guru; Gurdwara **Bangla Sahib**, Delhi |
| **9. Guru Tegh Bahadur** | 1665–1675 | Beheaded at Delhi — Gurdwara **Sis Ganj**; defended Kashmiri Pandits |
| **10. Guru Gobind Singh** | 1675–1708 | Founded the **Khalsa** (**1699**, Anandpur); five Ks; Guru Granth as eternal Guru |
| **Five Ks** | — | **Kesh**, kangha, kara, kachera, **kirpan** |
| **Hazur Sahib** | 1708 | Guru Gobind Singh's death at **Nanded** (Maharashtra); birthplace Patna Sahib |
| **Damdama Sahib** | — | Talwandi Sabo — final recension of the Guru Granth Sahib |

#### More Telugu Bhakti

| Poet / item | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Annamacharya** | 1408–1503 | Born at **Tallapaka**; sringara and adhyatma sankirtanas |
| **Sankirtana types** | — | **Adhyatma** (spiritual) and **sringara** (love) sankirtanas |
| **Kshetrayya** | 17th c. | Telugu **padam**s to Muvva Gopala; from **Movva** |
| **Tarigonda Vengamamba** | 1730–1817 | Woman poet-devotee of Venkateswara (Tirumala) |
| **Narayana Tirtha** | 17th c. | **Krishna Leela Tarangini** (tarangams) |
| **Siddhendra Yogi** | 17th c. | Shaped Kuchipudi; **Bhama Kalapam** |
| **Tyagaraja** | 1767–1847 | Lived at **Tiruvaiyaru** (Thanjavur); annual aradhana |
| **Vemana** | 17th c. | Refrain '**Viswadabhirama** Vinura Vema'; ataveladi metre |

**Don't confuse**
- **Adi Granth** compiled by **Guru Arjan** (1604); **Guru Granth Sahib** declared eternal Guru by **Guru Gobind Singh** (1708).
- **Akal Takht** = Guru Hargobind; **Khalsa** = Guru Gobind Singh; **Amritsar** = Guru Ramdas.
- **Kshetrayya** (padams, Movva) ≠ **Annamacharya** (sankirtanas, Tallapaka).

**TL;DR**
- Nanak (Talwandi, Sultanpur) → Angad (Gurmukhi) → Amardas (22 manjis) → Ramdas (Amritsar, Anand Karaj) → Arjan (Adi Granth 1604) → Hargobind (Miri-Piri, Akal Takht) → Har Rai → Har Krishan → Tegh Bahadur → Gobind Singh (Khalsa 1699).
- Five Ks; Damdama Sahib; Hazur Sahib (Nanded).
- Telugu: Annamacharya (Tallapaka; adhyatma/sringara), Kshetrayya (Movva), Vengamamba, Narayana Tirtha, Siddhendra Yogi (Bhama Kalapam), Tyagaraja (Tiruvaiyaru).
keyPoints: Guru Angad standardised Gurmukhi; Guru Amardas set up 22 manjis; Guru Ramdas founded Amritsar.
Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth (1604); Guru Hargobind introduced Miri-Piri and built the Akal Takht.
Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and introduced the five Ks (kesh, kangha, kara, kachera, kirpan).
Annamacharya was born at Tallapaka; Kshetrayya of Movva composed padams to Muvva Gopala.
Siddhendra Yogi shaped Kuchipudi and wrote Bhama Kalapam; Tyagaraja lived at Tiruvaiyaru.

items.title: For Mains — Bhakti Movement & Sufism
items.body:
**In one line:** For APPSC Mains Paper-II (medieval India — Islam, Bhakti and Sufi movements; and the AP cultural/Telugu-literature clauses), these movements are the case study of devotion as a force for social reform and composite culture.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | Caste oppression, ritualism, Islamic monotheism/Sufi influence, difficulty of Advaita |
| Features | Personal devotion, equality, vernacular, rejection of priestly mediation; Saguna vs Nirguna |
| Social impact | Attack on caste; women saints; Sufi khanqah service; Guru Nanak's Langar; Hindu-Muslim amity |
| Cultural impact | Flowering of vernacular literature and music; Amir Khusrau and qawwali; Sufi-yogi synthesis |
| AP significance | Telugu poet-saints — Annamacharya, Potana, Vemana, Ramadasu, Tyagaraja |
| Limitations / criticism | Reform was spiritual, not structural — caste as institution survived |

**Data points / names to quote**

- South-first (7th-12th c.): **63 Nayanars, 12 Alvars**; Acharyas **Shankara / Ramanuja / Madhva**; **Basavanna** (Lingayat, 12th c.).
- **Kabir, Guru Nanak** (Nirguna); **Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira** (Saguna); Varkari **Dnyaneshwar-Namdev-Eknath-Tukaram**.
- Sufi silsilahs: **Chishti** (Muinuddin, Ajmer; Nizamuddin Auliya), **Suhrawardi, Naqshbandi (Sirhindi), Qadiri (Miyan Mir)**.
- AP/Telugu: **Annamacharya (~32,000 sankirtanas, Tirupati)**, **Potana (Andhra Mahabhagavatamu)**, **Vemana Satakam**, **Ramadasu (Bhadrachalam, jailed by Golconda's Tanisha)**, **Tyagaraja**.

**The AP angle:** The Telugu Bhakti saints — especially **Ramadasu**, who served and was imprisoned by the **Golconda Qutb Shahis** — root this pan-Indian movement in Andhra's own soil and link it to the Deccan-sultanate story.

**Use in answers**

- Example: cite Kabir and Guru Nanak to show Bhakti-Sufi synthesis; use Ramadasu for the AP-specific angle.
- Quote: Vemana's 'Viswadabhirama Vinura Vema' as a people's voice against caste and hypocrisy.
- Diagram idea: a two-column map of Bhakti (Saguna/Nirguna) and Sufi (four silsilahs) streams converging on 'devotion + equality'.
keyPoints: Mains Paper-II clauses: M2-2 (Islam, Bhakti & Sufi) and M2-7/M2-2b (AP Telugu literature) — plus prelims P1-A-3.
Frame causes-features-social impact-cultural impact-AP significance-limitations.
Quote Nayanars/Alvars, Shankara-Ramanuja-Madhva, Kabir/Nanak, the four silsilahs, and the Varkari chain.
AP angle: Telugu saints Annamacharya, Potana, Vemana, Ramadasu (Golconda link), Tyagaraja.
Limitation: reform was spiritual not structural, yet it enriched vernaculars and pluralism.
